Swati, promise you won't laugh. I'm Madhav, and I am officially the biggest idiot in our batch.
So on Monday I get this message: "Congratulations! Your number has won a car in our anniversary lucky draw!" With a photo. A red hatchback. I actually screamed in the hostel corridor.
Did I enter a lucky draw? No. Did I think about that? Also no. I was already imagining driving home to Nagpur.
They said I just had to pay ₹4,999 "registration tax" to release the car. I paid. The next day, ₹12,000 for "insurance." That's when my brain finally woke up. What draw? What company? Why do I pay to win?
I called the number again. Switched off.
My roommate says the fee was the whole trick. There was never any car. The thrill just made me stop thinking for a day.
Anyway. We reported it on the cybercrime portal. Please don't tell the group.

qa.a: Which draw had actually been entered, whether the company was real, and why paying was needed to receive a prize.

Monday. A message popped up on Anirban's phone: "You have won the latest smartphone in our festive draw! Claim within 48 hours." Anirban grinned all through his lecture. His old phone's screen had been cracked for months.
Tuesday. The "prize desk" called. Friendly voice. Only a small ₹1,500 delivery tax, then the phone would ship. Anirban paid through the link right away. He felt lucky, chosen, for once.
Thursday. Another call. Customs had held the parcel. ₹6,000 more. Anirban hesitated.
His roommate Harish looked over his shoulder. "Which draw did you enter?"
Anirban opened his mouth. He hadn't entered any draw.
"And why would a prize need tax before delivery?" Harish asked quietly.
Anirban's excitement drained away. He felt stupid and angry at once. That evening they blocked the number and reported it on the cybercrime portal together.

When I was twenty, just married, a letter came to our house in Pune. Printed on thick paper with a gold stamp. "You have won ₹1 lakh in the International Lucky Draw." In those days, ₹1 lakh was a house.
I danced in the kitchen. I didn't ask myself which lucky draw I had entered. I hadn't entered anything.
The letter said to send ₹500 by money order for "processing tax." I took it from my savings tin and sent it that very day. Then another letter asked for ₹1,000. And another.
It was your Aajoba who finally asked, "Why must you pay to receive a gift?" I had no answer.
There was never any lakh. Only my ₹500 and my pride, gone. Since then, when luck asks for money first, I know it isn't luck.

The power had gone out across the colony, the rain was hammering on the window, and Vaibhav's phone was at twelve percent when the video call came.
A man in a police uniform, an office behind him with a flag. "This is the customs crime branch. A parcel in your name contains illegal drugs. You are under digital arrest. Do not disconnect. Do not tell anyone. If you tell your family, they will also be charged."
Vaibhav's hands went cold. He'd done nothing. But the man had his name, his Aadhaar number, his address.
For two hours, they kept him on camera. "To clear your name, transfer your savings to our verification account. It will be returned after checking."
He was typing in the account number when someone pounded on his door. His friend Asif, soaked. "Your phone's been busy for hours, I got worried!"
Vaibhav turned the screen toward him. Asif took one look and pressed "end call." "Real police don't arrest people on video. Come, we're reporting this now."

I'm Chaitanya, and I got caught by the oldest trick there is, on the most tired night of my life.
It was 1 a.m., the night before my board practical. I'd been studying for hours. A message popped up: "Your game account will be deleted in 30 minutes due to suspicious activity. Verify now." With a link.
My account had two years of progress. I didn't think. I tapped the link and typed my email and password.
Five minutes later, my account was gone, and the email password was changed too.
I felt sick. I'm the one who laughs at my uncle for forwarding fake messages.
In the morning I told my friend Eshaan. He didn't laugh. He said, "Tired plus panic, that's exactly when they get people." He helped me reset everything from the official site, and I told my father, who helped me report it.
Now I have a rule: nothing urgent after midnight.

I'm so annoyed with myself. At 11:40 tonight, after four hours of maths, a message came: "Congratulations Yash! You've won a new phone in the student lucky draw. Claim in 15 minutes!" It had my name. My actual name.

Ramesh, you rolled your eyes when I posted that scam warning in the family group. Let your Maria Aunty tell you why I do it.
When I was twenty, at college in Mangalore, I got an SMS: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Click to update KYC." It looked exactly like our bank's messages. I nearly clicked. Then I noticed the sender was a normal mobile number, and the link was misspelt.
I didn't just delete it. I rang the bank's official number, and they said it was fake. Then I thought of my grandfather, who had just learned to use a mobile. So I called home and told everyone.
Two days later, Grandpa got the same message. He remembered my call and didn't click. Our neighbour, who nobody warned, lost her pension that week.
That's why I post warnings, Ramesh. Someone less used to phones might be reading.

In their small flat in Berlin, Leila was cooking when her phone rang. "Frau Haddad? This is your bank's security team. There's a suspicious payment on your account. We've sent you a code. Please read it to me so we can cancel the transfer."
Leila stopped stirring. Ulla, her flatmate, looked up from the table.

"I'll call you back on the number on my card," Leila said.
"There's no time, madam. The money will be gone."
She hung up.
Her hands were a little unsteady, but she opened the bank's official app herself. No suspicious payment. Then she called the number printed on the back of her card. The real bank confirmed: they never ask customers for codes.
Ulla whistled. "I would have read it out."
"Nearly did," Leila admitted.

Asif, you asked why I don't like it when your friends say "everyone does it." Let your Sunaina Nani tell you.
When I was ten, a new girl came to our school. The older girls said, "Hide her tiffin. Everyone's doing it. If you don't, you're not one of us."

School counsellor's note, Class 10, Tuesday.
Ojas came to see me after the second period. His best friend Bhupen has been saying, "If you were really my friend, you'd bunk revision class with me," and then, "If you're really loyal, come to the mall during chemistry." Twice this week Ojas went. He missed a practical test.
He said, "If I say no, Bhupen tells everyone I've changed. The whole group ignores me. I'll lose all of them."
I could see how much this weighs on him. He kept rubbing his palms.
I told him that a friendship that needs proof by skipping class is using the friendship as leverage. Real friends can hear "no."
We practised a simple reply together: "I'm your friend. I'm also going to class." He also agreed to let me speak to his class teacher about the missed practical. I'll check in with him on Friday, and I've invited Bhupen for a chat too.

qa.q: What did Ojas miss after going to the mall?
qa.a: He missed a practical test.

qa.a: Ojas feels anxious and trapped, afraid the whole group will ignore him if he refuses.

qa.a: The counsellor named the pressure as leverage, practised a simple reply, spoke to his class teacher about the practical, and planned check-ins with Ojas and Bhupen.

qa.a: Bhupen may see his challenges as testing loyalty, not realising he is using the friendship to pressure Ojas.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager pressured to skip class to prove loyalty, fearing that refusing risks the whole group.

Saturday night, back home
At Deepak's birthday party tonight, the boys had a bottle someone's cousin brought. Deepak held a glass out to me. "Pankaj, if you're really my best friend, you'll have one. Just one. For me."
Everyone looked at me. My face went hot. I've known Deepak since Class 1. I didn't want to be the one who "ruined his birthday."
I said, "I'll have a cola, bro." Someone said, "Boring." Deepak looked at me like I'd let him down.
For the rest of the night, I stood near the snacks. Nobody talked to me much. It felt like I'd lost the whole group in one sentence.
When Papa picked me up, I told him what happened. He said, "That took guts. A real friend doesn't make you prove it like that." He's going to call Deepak's mother tomorrow, calmly.
I still feel horrible. But I think I'd do the same again.
Pankaj
